questions.q: What decision does schema mapping make, in the context of loading data into the star schema from Lesson 8?
options: Which source column becomes which target column before the load into tables like DimCustomer
How many fact tables the star schema should have
Which storage format the data warehouse should use
Whether to use a snowflake schema instead of a star schema
questions.explain: Before data lands in DimCustomer, DimProduct, or similar, something has to map each source column to its target column.

questions.q: What does an LLM typically attach to each proposed field mapping?
options: A confidence signal indicating how sure it is about that particular pair
A guaranteed correctness score of 100%
A legal disclaimer
Nothing — LLMs cannot propose mappings at all
questions.explain: High confidence typically reflects matching names and types; low confidence flags ambiguous columns like a generic 'status' field.

questions.q: Why is a wrong schema mapping considered worse than a wrong AI-generated test case?
options: A wrong test fails loudly and gets caught, while a wrong mapping ships silently and corrupts downstream data with no error thrown
Schema mappings are always more expensive to compute than tests
Wrong mappings are actually less risky than wrong tests
Test cases can never be verified, but mappings verify themselves
questions.explain: The asymmetry is the failure mode: a bad test is visible, a bad mapping is invisible until someone notices wrong numbers downstream.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend spot-checking even high-confidence proposed mappings, not just low-confidence ones?
options: A name-and-type match can still be a false positive if two columns are named similarly but mean different things
High-confidence mappings are always wrong
The LLM never assigns high confidence to any mapping
Spot-checking high-confidence pairs is required by law
questions.explain: Confidence based on naming and type similarity doesn't guarantee semantic correctness — real sample data is the actual check.

questions.q: What is the correct order of steps before a proposed schema mapping is used in an actual data load?
options: LLM proposes the mapping, human checks low-confidence pairs, human spot-checks high-confidence pairs, then the verified mapping feeds the load
The mapping is loaded immediately with no review
Only low-confidence pairs are ever checked; high-confidence ones are trusted blindly
The load happens first, then the mapping is proposed afterward
questions.explain: Only a mapping that has been checked against real sample data should feed the load into the target schema.
